# 

# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

Loki stores logs cheaply by indexing only a small set of labels (here service\_name and deployment\_environment) and keeping the log line itself unindexed. LogQL therefore works in two stages: a stream selector picks streams by label, then a pipeline filters lines, parses them (json, regexp, logfmt), filters on the extracted fields and reformats them. Wrapped in functions such as count\_over\_time() or rate(), the same pipeline becomes a metric query you can graph and alert on.  
In this lab you work only in your browser. The instructor's log shipper already sends easyTravel's JSON log lines to Loki. You select streams by label, filter lines, parse JSON and extract values with regex, compute error counts and rates per service, calculate a p95 from a number inside a log message, and build error count panels in Grafana — during the instructor's CreditCardCheckError500 cue.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can find and count the errors of any service from its logs within a minute. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You will extract fields from log lines at query time instead of waiting for new parsing rules. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Your error panels turn logs into metrics that can be charted and alerted on. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

A LogQL query is a stream selector followed by a pipeline. A metric query wraps it in a range function.  
*Figure: LogQL — {label selector} \|= line filter \| json / regexp parser \| field filter \| line\_format → Log Lines; Wrapped: count\_over\_time / rate / quantile\_over\_time( … \[range\]) → Metric Series*

| Stage | Syntax | Example | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Stream selector | {label="v", label=\~"re"} | {service\_name="easytravel-backend"} | Uses the index — always required |
| Line filter | \|= \!= \|\~ \!\~ | \|= "CreditCardCheck" | Fast text match before parsing |
| Parser \+ field filter | \| json · \| regexp "(?P\<x\>…)" · \| field op value | \| json \| level="ERROR" \| http\_status \>= 500 | Extracts fields at query time |
| Metric query | count\_over\_time / rate / quantile\_over\_time(… \[range\]) | sum by (service\_name) (count\_over\_time({…} \| json \| level="ERROR" \[5m\])) | Logs → numbers |

*Figure: Labels vs Extracted Fields — Few Indexed Labels (service\_name, deployment\_environment) Select Streams; Many Fields (level, trace\_id, message, http\_status, exception) Are Extracted by \| json at Query Time*

# 

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Streams, Labels and the Line

Loki groups log lines into streams; a stream is a unique set of labels. Labels are indexed, so they must be few and low in cardinality — here service\_name and deployment\_environment. Everything else stays in the line (or in structured metadata such as trace and span IDs) and is extracted at query time by parsers. This is why Loki is cheap to run — and why every query must start with a selective stream selector.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| Query-time parsing means you can ask a new question of old logs without changing any ingestion rule. |
|  |
| Log metrics (count\_over\_time, rate) let you put "errors per service" on the same dashboard as Prometheus metrics, with the same time picker. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Line Filters vs Field Filters

A line filter (\|= "ERROR") is a fast text search on the raw line; it can match the word anywhere, including inside other fields. A field filter after a parser (\| json \| level="ERROR") compares the extracted value exactly but costs more, because every line must be parsed. Best practice: narrow with a cheap line filter first, then parse and filter on fields for precision.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With LogQL |
| :---- |
| A team adds trace\_id and http\_status as Loki labels "to make searches faster" — ingestion slows down, the index explodes and queries time out. |
|  |
| REASON: Every new label value creates a new stream; trace IDs are unique per request. |
|  |
| YOU MUST keep labels for where logs come from (service, environment, cluster), and extract what is in the log with parsers or keep it as structured metadata. |

## 3.3  Log Metric Functions

| Function | Returns | Example | Use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| count\_over\_time(…\[r\]) | Lines per stream in the range | count\_over\_time({…} \| json \| level="ERROR" \[5m\]) | Error counts |
| rate(…\[r\]) | Lines per second | rate({service\_name="checkout"} \[1m\]) | Log throughput |
| quantile\_over\_time(q, … \| unwrap x \[r\]) | Percentile of an extracted number | quantile\_over\_time(0.95, … \| unwrap ms \[10m\]) | Latency from logs |
| sum / topk … by (label) | Aggregation like PromQL | topk(3, sum by (exception) (…)) | Ranking |

| 📝  How to Decide Between a Label and an Extracted Field |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Does this value identify where the logs come from and have only a few possible values?" Then it can be a label (service, environment, cluster, namespace). If it describes the event (level, status, user, trace ID, message), keep it in the line or structured metadata and extract it with a parser in the query. |

| **1.A  How many streams exist, and why is "level" not a label?**  Answer:  **Number of streams:** There are **2 streams**—one for `easytravel-frontend` and one for `easytravel-backend` under `deployment_environment="cohort"`. **Why `level` is not a label:** Loki creates a separate indexed stream for every unique combination of label values. Keeping `level` inside the JSON log line instead of indexing it as a label prevents multiplying the number of streams, keeping the index compact and queries fast.  |
| **1.B  The line filter \|= "500" matched lines from two services. Why could a line filter match more than you intend?**  Answer:  **Why `|= "500"` can match more than intended:** A line filter performs a plain-text substring match across the entire raw log line before any parsing happens. Because it is unaware of JSON field boundaries, `"500"` will also match lines where `500` appears inside a `duration_ms` value (e.g., `500 ms`), a `trace_id`, or free-text message details rather than `http_status`. Parsing with `| json` and filtering on `| http_status >= 500` avoids these false positives.  |

| TASK 2 — JSON PARSER: Extract, Filter and Reformat |
| :---- |

| 2 | Parse JSON Logs and Filter on Extracted Fields*Loki LogQL SOP — Day 4 — Lab 3* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

The json parser turns every key of the log line into a field you can filter on, aggregate by and print. You filter errors precisely, combine line and field filters, print a readable line with line\_format, and extract only the fields you need.

| ⌨  Task 2 — \| json |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Q1 — precise error filter on the extracted level |
| {deployment\_environment="cohort"} \| json \| level="ERROR" ![][image13] ![][image14] |
| \# Q2 — cheap line filter first, then parse, then numeric field filter |
| {deployment\_environment="cohort"} \|= "http\_status" \| json \| http\_status \>= 500 ![][image15] ![][image16] |
| \# Q3 — readable output with line\_format |
| {service\_name="easytravel-frontend"} \| json \| level="ERROR" \| line\_format "{{.ts}} {{.level}} {{.message}}" ![][image17] ![][image18] |
| \# Q4 — extract only two fields under new names |
| {service\_name="easytravel-backend"} \| json lvl="level", msg="message" \| lvl="ERROR" \| line\_format "{{.lvl}}: {{.msg}}" ![][image19] ![][image20] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Q1: ERROR lines from the backend and the frontend (JSON as written) |
| Q2: lines whose http\_status is 500 — backend "Booking failed …" and frontend "POST /checkout \-\> 500" |
| Q3: 2026-…T… ERROR POST /checkout \-\> 500 (… ms) |
| Q4: ERROR: Booking failed: CreditCardCheckError500 … |
| **2.A  Why does Q2 put \|= "http\_status" before \| json? What would happen without it on a busy system?**  Answer: **Why `|= "http_status"` comes before `| json`:** The cheap plain-text line filter (`|= "http_status"`) executes first and immediately drops log lines that do not contain `"http_status"` before the more CPU-intensive JSON parser runs. **What happens without it on a busy system:** Loki would have to deserialize and parse every single JSON log line in the stream first before evaluating `http_status >= 500`, making the query significantly slower and much more resource-intensive.  |

| TASK 3 — REGEX & LOG METRICS: count\_over\_time(), rate(), unwrap |
| :---- |

| 3 | Use the Regex Parser and Turn Logs into Metrics*Loki LogQL SOP — Day 4 — Lab 3* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

The regexp parser extracts values that are inside free text — here the duration in "Booking completed in 412 ms". Metric queries wrap a log pipeline in a range function and aggregate like PromQL. You count errors per service, compute their rate, rank exceptions, and calculate a booking p95 from the log messages.

| ⌨  Task 3 — Metric queries (instant, last 10 minutes) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Q5 — errors per service (count) and per second (rate); run as Instant queries (Query options → Type: Instant), range Last 15 minutes |
| sum by (service\_name) (count\_over\_time({deployment\_environment="cohort"} \| json \| level="ERROR" \[10m\])) ![][image22] |
| sum by (service\_name) (rate({deployment\_environment="cohort"} \| json \| level="ERROR" \[5m\])) ![][image23] |
| \# Q6 — the most frequent exception |
| topk(1, sum by (exception) (count\_over\_time({deployment\_environment="cohort"} \| json \| exception\!="" \[10m\]))) ![][image24] |
| \# Q7 — regex parser \+ unwrap: p95 of "Booking completed in N ms" |
| quantile\_over\_time(0.95, {service\_name="easytravel-backend"} \|= "Booking completed" \| regexp "Booking completed in (?P\<ms\>\[0-9\]+) ms" \| unwrap ms \[10m\]) by (service\_name) ![][image25] |
| \# CUE C2 — when the instructor announces "CreditCardCheckError500 OFF", write the time down ![][image26] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Q5: one value per service (easytravel-backend, easytravel-frontend) — similar counts, because each failed booking logs an error in both |
|     rate: a small number of errors per second while the fault was ON |
| Q6: the credit-card exception (for example CreditCardCheckException) with its count |
| Q7: one number in milliseconds for the backend (successful bookings only) |
| **3.A  Record Q5 and Q7. Why do the two services report almost the same number of errors?**   Answer:  **Recorded Q5 & Q7 Values: Q5 (`count_over_time` / `rate`):** Both `easytravel-backend` and `easytravel-frontend` reported nearly identical error counts during the fault window (and a corresponding small non-zero error rate per second). *(Insert your exact numeric counts and Q7 millisecond value read from Grafana Explore.)* **Q7 (`quantile_over_time` on `unwrap ms`):** Returned the backend p95 booking completion duration in milliseconds (for example, \~`400 ms` – `650 ms` for successful `"Booking completed in N ms"` lines). **Why both services report almost the same number of errors:** Each failed checkout request propagates across both tiers, writing one `ERROR` log line in `easytravel-backend` (`Booking failed: CreditCardCheckError500...`) and one paired `ERROR` log line in `easytravel-frontend` (`POST /checkout -> 500...`). Any slight difference in counts is only due to timestamps landing right on the boundary of the `[10m]` evaluation window.  |
| **3.B  Compare Q7 with the Prometheus checkout p95. Why can a p95 from logs differ from a p95 from a histogram?**  Answer: **Why log-based p95 differs from Prometheus histogram p95: Population difference (subset vs. all requests):** Q7 explicitly filters with `|= "Booking completed"`, which measures only successful bookings (`HTTP 200`) and excludes slow `HTTP 500` failed checkouts, whereas the Prometheus `http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket` histogram records **all** requests (both fast successes and slow `1.1s–2.3s` failures). **Exact values vs. bucket interpolation:** LogQL `quantile_over_time` computes the percentile from exact per-request millisecond integers unwrapped from each log line, while Prometheus `histogram_quantile` estimates the percentile by linearly interpolating across fixed bucket boundaries (`le="0.5"`, `0.75`, `1.0`, `1.5`, `2.5`, etc.).  |

| **📟  Expected Output** |

| Panel 2: a number above 0 (orange / red above the thresholds) |
| Panel 3: the credit-card exception with its count |

| **4.A  Compare Panel 1 with the Prometheus "Error ratio by route" panel. What does each show that the other does not?**  Answer:  **What Loki Panel 1 (`Error log lines per service`) shows that Prometheus does not:** It displays the **raw volume (count) of `ERROR` log lines** grouped by `service_name` (`easytravel-backend` and `easytravel-frontend`) across time intervals, showing cross-service error propagation and log-level failures even for events that might not map directly to an HTTP route. **What the Prometheus `Error ratio by route` panel shows that Loki Panel 1 does not:** It displays the **normalized failure rate (percentage/ratio of failed requests to total traffic)** broken down by **individual HTTP route** (`/checkout`, `/search`, `/booking`, `/`) and separated by status class (`4xx` vs. `5xx`), showing how severe the errors are relative to total request volume.  |
| **4.B  Why does Panel 3 use an instant query with \[\$\_\_range\], and Panel 1 a range query with \[\$\_\_auto\]?**  Answer:  **Panel 3 (`Top exceptions`) — Instant query with `[$__range]`:** `[$__range]` spans the entire selected dashboard time window as a single interval, and **Instant** mode evaluates the query once at the end of that window so the table displays one total aggregate count per exception over the whole selected period rather than repeating rows for every timestamp step. **Panel 1 (`Error log lines per service`) — Range query with `[$__auto]`:** **Range** mode evaluates the query repeatedly at every step across the graph's timeline, and `[$__auto]` automatically sets each evaluation bucket width to match the graph's step resolution so every bar represents the exact error count for its own time slice without overlapping or leaving gaps.  |

# 

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Labels list empty | Loki data source missing, or the time range is outside the log window | Connections → Data sources → Loki (look only); Explore time range Last 1 hour | Choose Last 1 hour; tell the instructor if Loki is missing |
| Only INFO lines, no errors | Cue C1 not yet given or just given | Check the cue time you wrote down | Wait 2 minutes after cue C1 and widen the range to 30 minutes |
| \| json gives \_\_error\_\_=JSONParserErr | A line is not JSON | Add \| \_\_error\_\_="" to drop them | Check which service wrote non-JSON lines |
| Metric query returns "No data" or many points instead of one | Query type Range instead of Instant, or range shorter than the log interval | Query options → Type | Use Instant for single values; widen the range |
| Panel shows no data after saving | Time range does not include the fault window | Time picker | Select a range that includes cues C1 to C2 |
| Grafana: Loki data source missing | Provisioning file not loaded | ls grafana/provisioning/datasources | Restart grafana after adding loki.yml |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Labels vs Fields |
| :---- |
| Without notes: which easyTravel keys are labels, structured metadata or extracted fields — and why? |
| What happens to Loki if trace\_id becomes a label? |
|  |
| Key answer to explore: service/env labels; trace/span IDs as metadata; level, message, http\_status parsed; ID labels explode streams. |
| **Discussion 2 — Filter Order** |
| Rewrite Q2 without the line filter. When does the order matter? |
| How do line filters compare with Splunk search terms before the pipe? |
|  |
| Key insight: cheap text filters first, parsing later — same idea as filtering early in SPL and DQL. |
| **Discussion 3 — Logs as Metrics** |
| When would you alert on a LogQL metric instead of a Prometheus metric? |
| What are the risks (cost, delay, log volume changes)? |
|  |
| Key answer: when only logs contain the signal (specific message, exception); watch query cost and logging changes. |
| **Discussion 4 — LogQL vs the Others** |
| Translate Q5 to SPL, DQL and NRQL. |
| Which syntax felt most natural? |
|  |
| Answer: stats count by service · summarize count(), by: {service.name} · SELECT count(\*) FROM Log FACET service.name. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| IDs as labels | Hoping for faster search | Stream explosion | Labels for origin only |
| Parsing everything | Convenience | Slow queries | Line filter before \| json |
| Instant queries for log lines | Using /query | Errors | query\_range for logs |
| Fixed ranges in panels | Copying from shell | Wrong counts when zooming | \[\$\_\_auto\] / \[\$\_\_range\] |
| Forgetting \_\_error\_\_ | Mixed formats | Confusing results | \| \_\_error\_\_="" after parsers |

# 

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — LOKI LOGQL COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Selector | {service\_name="easytravel-backend"} · {service\_name=\~"a\|b"} | Streams |
| Line filters | \|= "x" · \!= "x" · \|\~ "re" · \!\~ "re" | Text |
| JSON | \| json · \| json a="key" | Extract fields |
| Field filter | \| level="ERROR" · \| http\_status \>= 500 | After parser |
| Regex | \| regexp "in (?P\<ms\>\[0-9\]+) ms" | Named groups |
| Format | \| line\_format "{{.service}} {{.message}}" | Output |
| Errors drop | \| \_\_error\_\_="" | Parsing errors |
| Count | count\_over\_time({…} \[5m\]) | Lines per range |
| Rate | rate({…} \[1m\]) | Lines per second |
| Unwrap | quantile\_over\_time(0.95, … \| unwrap ms \[10m\]) | Numbers from logs |
| Grafana ranges | \[\$\_\_auto\] · \[\$\_\_range\] | Panels |
| Where | Grafana → Explore → Loki → Code mode (query type Instant for metric queries) | Browser |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — learners never run these commands. Do this once, at least 30 minutes before the cohort. All commands run on the shared lab host; learners only use Grafana in the browser.  
1\. Start Loki and the easyTravel JSON log feed (Day 4 setup note: loki/docker-compose.yml and loki/et\_json\_log\_feed.py). The feed writes JSON lines with the keys ts, level, service, message, route, http\_status, duration\_ms, exception, trace\_id and span\_id, and sends them to Loki with the labels service\_name (easytravel-frontend, easytravel-backend) and deployment\_environment=cohort. It writes error lines whenever the fault flag file reads on.

| ⌨  Instructor — Loki, feed and cues |
| :---- |
|  |
| docker compose \-f loki/docker-compose.yml up \-d |
| nohup python3 loki/et\_json\_log\_feed.py \--loki http\://localhost:3100 \--flag \~/obs-lab/control/fault.flag & |
| \# Check Loki is ready and the feed arrives (expected: ready, then two label values) |
| curl \-s localhost:3100/ready; curl \-s localhost:3100/loki/api/v1/label/service\_name/values |
| \# C1  start of Task 1 (about T+4): announce "CreditCardCheckError500 ON" and the time |
| ./faultctl.sh on |
| \# C2  end of Task 3 (about T+22): announce "OFF" and the time |
| ./faultctl.sh off |

2\. In Grafana (admin): Connections → Data sources → Add Loki (URL http\://\<loki-host\>:3100, no authentication, reachable only inside the lab network). Make it read-only for learners (Viewer / Editor in their own folder only).  
3\. faultctl.sh switches the easyTravel plug-in CreditCardCheckError500 and also writes the flag file that the log feed reads, so metrics, traces and logs show the same fault window.  
4\. At the end of the lab confirm the fault is OFF; keep Loki running for Labs 4–5 reviews.
